JSON: Name: publisher_ai_services_rct Title: Randomized controlled trial to measure the causal effect of tailored publisher-provided AI services on researchers' AI adoption, beneficial use, and attitudes Short Hypothesis: Provision of tailored AI services by a publisher causally increases the proportion of researchers who report benefitting from using AI in their research by at least 20 percentage points within six months, compared with no intervention. Related Work: Existing work documents cross-sectional variation in researcher attitudes and self-reported AI use using survey-based segmentation and k-means clustering, revealing profiles that vary by discipline, career stage, region, institutional policy, and self-assessed AI understanding. Prior empirical studies on technology adoption in academia and digital interventions have shown heterogeneous uptake and attitudinal change following training, tooling access, or informational campaigns. Randomized evaluations of digital tool rollouts in scholarly workflows are rare; most evidence is observational or based on one-off pilots with self-selected participants. Limitations in prior approaches include reliance on self-reported outcomes, cross-sectional designs that preclude causal inference, limited measurement of behavioral usage (versus attitudes), aggregation that masks heterogenous effects across researcher segments, and sparse component-level evaluation (which service features drive change). No published work robustly tests publisher-delivered bundles of services (tool access, training, policy templates) with stratified randomized assignment and pre-registered analyses to measure causal impacts on both behavior and attitudes. Abstract: This study tests whether publisher-delivered, profile-tailored AI services cause increases in researchers' beneficial AI use and measurable shifts in attitudes. We will run a multi-arm randomized controlled trial with stratified assignment by pre-identified researcher profile (e.g., pioneers, challengers, neutrals). Interventions include (a) a control (no new services), (b) a generic information package, and (c) a tailored service bundle combining tool access (privacy-guaranteed AI tools and translation/editing assistants), role-specific training modules, and institutional policy templates. Primary contributions are (1) causal estimates of publisher interventions on self-reported and logged AI use, (2) component-level effects via embedded ablations, and (3) analysis of heterogeneous treatment effects across researcher profiles, disciplines, and career stages. Expected outcomes are precise effect-size estimates for uptake and attitude change, informing publishers and institutions about which service elements produce measurable, generalizable benefits and which researcher segments require alternative approaches. Experiments: Dataset and recruitment: recruit N=2400 academic researchers sampled to cover disciplines (Humanities, Social Sciences, STM), career stages (early, mid, late), regions (North America, UK, Rest of World) and balanced across the eight attitudinal profiles from the baseline survey instrument. Inclusion: active researchers with at least one publication in the past five years. Baseline: replicate the 26-item attitudinal battery, demographics, institutional policy status, and self-reported AI tool use; collect consent for anonymous behavioral logging for provided tools. Randomization: stratified random assignment within each profile x discipline cell to three primary arms (Control, Generic Info, Tailored Services) with equal allocation (n≈800 per arm). Tailored Services arm contains three components: A) privacy-forward tool access (machine translation, editing/chatbot research assistant with audit logs), B) role-specific online training modules (micro-modules tailored to profile and discipline), C) publisher policy templates and recommended best-practice workflows. Ablation sub-randomization: within Tailored Services arm, randomly vary presence/absence of components (A only, B only, C only, A+B, A+C, B+C, A+B+C) to isolate component effects. Timelines: baseline, 3-month interim survey and usage extraction, 6-month primary endpoint survey and usage extraction. Baselines for comparison: Control (status quo) and Generic Info (static brochure and links). Evaluation metrics: Primary outcome: proportion reporting they have 'benefitted' from AI use (binary) at 6 months; secondary outcomes: frequency of AI tool use (logged sessions per month), Beneficial Use Index (composite numeric score of editing/translation/analysis benefits), Trust score (Likert composite), Concern score (Likert composite), incidence of reported problematic outputs (hallucinations/plagiarism), and objective indicators: number of edits derived from tool logs, number of manuscript submissions (self-reported). Statistical analysis: pre-registered difference-in-means and logistic regression models adjusted for baseline score and stratification variables; mixed-effects models with random intercepts for institution; difference-in-differences for usage metrics; heterogeneity analysis by profile, discipline, career stage, and institutional policy status; multiple-testing correction via Benjamini-Hochberg. Ablation analysis: compare component arms using linear contrasts and interaction terms. Power and sample size: with N≈800 per arm, assuming baseline beneficial_use_rate=0.36, alpha=0.05, two-sided test, the design provides >90% power to detect an absolute increase of 10 percentage points and >80% power to detect a 7 percentage point increase; the design is powered to detect moderate heterogenous effects across major profiles. Data collection and instruments: replicate validated attitudinal items from baseline report, standardized usage logging schema for tool interactions, and pre-defined coding rules for self-reported open responses. Pre-registration: all outcomes, analysis code, and data-release plan pre-registered before randomization. Risk Factors and Limitations: Selection bias: recruited sample may not represent broader researcher population; self-selection into participation may correlate with baseline attitudes. Contamination: control-group participants may access external AI resources or discuss interventions with treatment participants, diluting estimated effects. Self-report bias: primary outcomes include self-assessments susceptible to social desirability and recall error; behavioral logs will cover only provided tools. Engagement variability: low uptake of offered services can produce null effects despite efficacy if not used. Measurement validity: 'benefit' is subjective and may not map to objective research quality; objective proxies (submission counts, citation accrual) require long follow-up beyond 6 months. Privacy and ethical constraints: logging and tool access require robust privacy guarantees; some researchers may refuse logging, reducing effective sample. Heterogeneity and generalization: effects may vary across disciplines, regions, career stages, and institutional policies; results may not generalize to contexts with different institutional norms or AI market maturity. Technical failure modes: tool outages, incorrect logging, or poor integration can bias usage metrics. Resource constraints: provisioning privacy-forward AI tools and training at scale requires compute and operational resources; component ablations increase sample fragmentation and reduce per-condition power for smaller subgroups. Regulatory and legal: intellectual property and data protection regulations across jurisdictions may constrain tool features or data collection, limiting intervention fidelity.
